It awaits run() from tests/helpers/project.mjs, and run() resolves only on the child process&#39;s &#39;close&#39; event. Every assertion runs after that, against the exit code, stdout, the PNG files, or report.json. The `sleep(args.settle)` call is inside the inspect tool (skills/presentation/templates/bootstrap/scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs), not inside a test. The tool calls it only after `page.waitForFunction` has polled `data-step-index` up to the target step, with STEP_TIMEOUT. That settle interval is a capture feature of the tool, and the test checks it (`settledMs &gt;= SETTLE`). The test does not use it as a substitute for waiting on state. The `sleep` in preview.mjs is a helper of the tool, not a wait inside a test. source_audits{"demo-integration":[[{"id":"demo-scene-kit-api-use","classification":"confirmed","rationale":"Talk.tsx renders the kit&#39;s Presentation with steps, title, initialMode and className, and builds no navigation, chrome or stage of its own. scene.tsx imports AnimatePresence, Appear, Arrow, Box, Emphasis, Frame, Label, SceneLayer and SymbolChip from presentation-kit and builds the whole scene from them. Every step module is a Step&lt;SampleState&gt; with Scene: SampleScene. Stage.tsx calls Scene with payload, stepId and stepIndex, which matches the SceneProps contract in types.ts. The demo reimplements no stage scaling, layoutId handling or scene keying. consensus{"demo-integration":[{"id":"demo-scene-kit-api-use","basis":"consensus-pass","votes":[{"id":"demo-scene-kit-api-use","verdict":"pass","rationale":"Talk.tsx renders the kit&#39;s &lt;Presentation&gt; with steps, title, initialMode and className, and does not rebuild navigation, chrome or stage. The shared SampleScene in scene.tsx draws everything with kit primitives (SceneLayer, Appear, AnimatePresence, Box, Label, Arrow, SymbolChip, Emphasis, Frame), all imported from presentation-kit. It also recorded the default attribution and empty brand slot, and a two-step probe of grouped-scene persistence, the 600 ms newcomer delay and the departing exit. Rounds 0–2 exercised build, verify with the render loop on 127.0.0.1, delayed console-error failure naming step 9, and missing-Chromium recovery. Header.tsx always renders data-presentation-marker, which shows the step number (formatStepNumber) and the era label as visible text in the header&#39;s marker row. It is not limited to one mode, and the sample CSS (style.css 33-46) styles it but never hides it in present mode. Footer.tsx always renders &lt;h2 data-presentation-title&gt;{step.title}&lt;/h2&gt;. The caption, the prev/next buttons and the progress list sit inside `mode === &#39;browse&#39; &amp;&amp; (...)`, so they are not rendered in present mode. Presentation.tsx renders &lt;Toc&gt; only when `mode === &#39;browse&#39; &amp;&amp; wide`. The focused test &#39;present mode shows marker and one-line title but hides caption, ToC, and prev/next&#39; sets up present mode. It asserts that the marker and the title heading are present and that caption, toc, nav and progress are null. Judges B and C reached this verdict, and I rule pass with them. Judge A&#39;s reason does not decide the criterion. The requirement&#39;s &#39;one-line title&#39; is used in its plain sense: the step&#39;s single title line, in contrast to the multi-line caption that browse mode shows. That title is rendered. Neither the requirement nor its review guidance calls for a CSS no-wrap or single-line constraint, or for a test that checks line count. Both are rejected by `!Number.isInteger(count) || count &lt; 1`, which throws a render VerifyError. So an unreadable count cannot step through zero steps and pass. (2) Transition check: the check is `getAttribute(&#39;data-step-index&#39;) === String(n)`, a strict string comparison. An absent (null) or non-numeric index never equals the expected string, so it is never counted as progress. Nothing here converts with Number(null) the way the guidance warns against. Step 0 is the starting state, not a transition, so not checking it does not count anything as progress. (3) A failure to render or advance throws `VerifyError(&#39;render&#39;, ..., step+1)`, which names the step. verify.mjs prints `VERIFY FAIL [render] step N` and sets `process.exitCode = 1`. (4) The required focused test exists. It injects a fault that stops the step index from advancing past 3. It asserts a non-zero exit code, stderr matching `VERIFY FAIL [render] step 5`, and the text &#39;did not advance&#39;. No test that drives a browser contains a fixed sleep of its own. The e2e tests (verify-pass, verify-failures) and the integration test (inspect.test.mjs) start the scripts through run(). run() awaits the child&#39;s &#39;close&#39; event (project.mjs 15-28), and the tests assert on exit code, stdout/stderr and report.json only after that has resolved. The browser stepping those tests exercise waits on observable state: each ArrowRight is followed by page.waitForFunction until data-step-index equals the target index, with a timeout. That is in render.mjs 47-58 and in the inspect helper 164-171. The render-errors unit test injects a virtual-clock `sleep` that only advances a counter (render-errors.test.mjs 20-25), so it does not wait in real time. The setTimeouts in verify-failures.test.mjs are inside the fixture scene code that injects late errors, not waits in the test. Judge C fails the criterion because inspect.test.mjs passes `--settle 700` and checks settledMs &gt;= 700. That flag tests the helper&#39;s own capture-settle feature, which is product behaviour. The helper runs that settle only after waitForFunction has confirmed the step index, so the test does not use a fixed sleep in place of waiting for the step state. The review guidance also excludes settle-delay tuning from scoring. No test hardcodes a preview port. The tests start the verify and inspect scripts, which call startPreview(root) with no port. startPreview then picks one through freePort(), which listens on port 0 and reads the assigned port (preview.mjs 7-16, 45-46). The preview child is the vite process itself (process.execPath with vite.js), not an npm or npx wrapper. stop() sends SIGTERM to that child and awaits its &#39;close&#39;. A process &#39;exit&#39; hook also SIGKILLs it as a backstop (preview.mjs 48-77). verify.mjs closes the browser and stops the preview in a finally block (58-61), and the inspect helper does the same (185-188). The tests check this cleanup: they assert portOpen(previewPort(output)) is false after the passing run (verify-pass.test.mjs 28-32) and after every failure mode (verify-failures.test.mjs 19-25). Judge C fails the criterion because run()&#39;s 240 s timeout guard SIGKILLs only the npm process. That guard runs only if a script hangs for 240 s, and no recorded run does. Every wait inside verify is bounded (readiness 20 s, step 5 s, and per-step settles), and the finally block stops the vite child that verify itself spawned. The tests&#39; own cleanup path never kills a wrapper while leaving a preview it started running. None of them drives Playwright directly and none sleeps. Each one awaits run() from tests/helpers/project.mjs. run() resolves only on the child&#39;s &#39;close&#39; event, and the assertions run after that: on exit code, stdout and stderr, report.json, or the port being closed. The only setTimeout in the helper is the 240 s safety kill timer, not a wait before an assertion. In verify-failures.test.mjs the setTimeouts at lines 82 and 98 are strings injected into the fixture scene source to make the page throw errors late. They are not waits in the test. render-errors.test.mjs drives a fake page whose injected `sleep` only advances a virtual clock (lines 20-25). browser-launch.test.mjs uses stubs. Inside the inspect helper the tests run, each step is captured only after page.waitForFunction polls data-step-index to the target step with a timeout. Judge C points to the `--settle 700` argument and the helper&#39;s `sleep(args.settle)`. That settle delay is a feature of the inspect tool, which captures after a settle interval. It runs only after the step index has been confirmed by polling, and it is not a sleep in a test used in place of waiting for state. The test asserts only after the process closes, and settledMs &gt;= SETTLE checks the helper&#39;s behavior. So C&#39;s reason does not show a browser test sleeping instead of waiting for state. The test files are quoted in full, and ports appear only through portOpen and previewPort, which parse the dynamically chosen port from output. The tests start previews and browsers only through the verify and inspect scripts. Every copy of those scripts calls startPreview(root) with no port. The repository&#39;s scripts/lib/preview.mjs and the template&#39;s preview.mjs both use freePort(), which listens on port 0 and reads the assigned port, then pass it with --strictPort. They spawn the vite binary directly through process.execPath, not through an npm or npx wrapper. stop() sends SIGTERM to that child and awaits &#39;close&#39;. A process &#39;exit&#39; handler also SIGKILLs the child. The repository verify, the template verify and the template inspect (used by inspect.test) all close the browser and await preview.stop() in a finally block. The e2e tests assert the preview port is closed after both passing and failing runs. Judge C argues that run()&#39;s SIGKILL timeout kills only the npm wrapper. That timer fires only if a run hangs past 240 s. It is a safety net, not how the tests stop the preview. On every run the tests perform, the script stops its own directly spawned vite child before exiting. No test relies on killing a wrapper to stop the preview, so C&#39;s hypothetical does not show a test leaving a preview running. In both the repository and template copies of preview.mjs, startPreview then calls freePort(), which listens on port 0 and passes the assigned port with --strictPort. Second, every started process is terminated. The preview runs as the vite.js binary spawned directly through process.execPath, not through an npm or npx wrapper. Its stop() sends SIGTERM and awaits &#39;close&#39;, and a process &#39;exit&#39; handler SIGKILLs it as a fallback. The repository verify, template verify and template inspect each close the browser and await preview.stop() in a finally block. The npm processes the tests start exit on their own, and run() awaits their close. The e2e tests assert the preview port is closed after both passing and failing runs. The test files are quoted in full, and ports appear only through portOpen and previewPort, which parse the dynamically chosen port from output. The tests start previews and browsers only through the verify and inspect scripts. Every copy of those scripts calls startPreview(root) with no port. The repository&#39;s scripts/lib/preview.mjs and the template&#39;s preview.mjs both use freePort(), which listens on port 0 and reads the assigned port, then pass it with --strictPort. They spawn the vite binary directly through process.execPath, not through an npm or npx wrapper. stop() sends SIGTERM to that child and awaits &#39;close&#39;. A process &#39;exit&#39; handler also SIGKILLs the child. The repository verify, the template verify and the template inspect (used by inspect.test) all close the browser and await preview.stop() in a finally block. The e2e tests assert the preview port is closed after both passing and failing runs. Judge C argues that run()&#39;s SIGKILL timeout kills only the npm wrapper. In browse mode, active progress/ToC entries exposed `aria-current=\"step\"` and `data-presentation-active=\"true\"`.
